newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish parade held amid Catholic protests.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish parade held amid Catholic protests.

text.p: A disputed Protestant march went ahead in Londonderry on Saturday to noisy protests but no violence from a crowd of several hundred Catholic demosntrators.

In suits and bowler hats, the Apprentice Boys, a Protestant order of mostly middle-aged men, marched along the walls of Northern Ireland's second city to catcalls of "racists" and "IRA" from a crowd of about 200 Catholic demonstrators.

Police manhandled two members of the Bogside Residents Association, an Irish nationalist grouping, who tried to stand in the way of the marchers as they went on a circuit of the city's 17th century walls.

The Apprentice Boys was formed to commemorate 13 young Protestant apprentices who slammed the gates of the ancient City of Derry on the advancing Catholic forces of James II in December 1688, triggering a siege which ended in August when Protestant forces relieved the city.

The march had aroused fears of a re-run of Northern Ireland sectarian violence which prevented it taking place in August. But there was no violence, only a torrent of slogans from Catholics hemmed in by hundreds of police and prevented from reaching the city walls.
The Bogside Residents Association, which says such marches are sectarian and intimidatory, wanted to place 13 protesters along the walls to stage a peaceful demonstration against the parade.
But they refused in negotiations with police to stand beside the walls and let the march go past.
"We will not be dictated to. The RUC (Royal Ulster Constabulary police) is not going to tell us how to conduct a democratic protest," said the chairman of the association Donncha MacNaillais.
Senior police asked him and a fellow demonstrator if they would promise to stand to one side but they refused and were removed forcibly by police.
Within minutes, some 200 Apprentice Boys marched to the beat of a drum along the controversial section to start their parade along the mile-long circuit.
The incident happened at a flashpoint where high stone ramparts are just yards from a street of Catholic residents.

Catholics, who oppose British rule and want an all-Ireland state, say Apprentice Boys and other staunchly Protestant pro-British organisations try to lord it over them by holding parades throughout the province every year.
The Apprentice Boys and the other so-called "loyal orders" deny wishing to give any insult to the Catholic minority.
They say marches are a civil right and a cornerstone of a public manifestation of their allegiance to the British Monarchy.
Sectarian bitterness and violence erupted in mid-summer, at the height of the Protestant annual marching season, with trouble in Belfast, Londonderry, Portadown and other towns.
In August the British government blocked the controversial section of Londonderry's walls to Apprentice Boys who wanted to parade it on August 12, the biggest day in their march calendar.
The organisation declared that they would walk the parade subsequently "at a time of our own choosing".
On Friday, Catholic nationalist leader and Londonderry legislator John Hume urged Catholics to allow the Protestants to walk unhindered, and call off their protest.
